title: P'an Ku: A Taoist Creation Account
subtitle: A later cosmogony and its editorial frame

learningObjectives.text: How does P'an Ku make the world?

creation.author: E. T. C. Werner (modern compiler and author)
creation.translator: not applicable; authored in English by E. T. C. Werner
creation.locator: Chapter III · Cosmogony-p'an Ku and the Creation Myth; Chapter III · Cosmogony-p'an Ku and the Creation Myth, normalized characters 1680-2330
creation.excerpt: His task occupied eighteen thousand years, during which he formed the sun, moon, and stars, the heavens and the earth, himself increasing in stature day by day, being daily six feet taller than the day before, until, his labours ended, he died that his works might live. His head became the mountains, his breath the wind and clouds, his voice the thunder, his limbs the four quarters of the earth, his blood the rivers, his flesh the soil, his beard the constellations, his skin and hair the herbs and trees, his teeth, bones, and marrow the metals, rocks, and precious stones, his sweat the rain, and the insects creeping over his body human beings
creation.note: Quotation from E. T. C. Werner's 1922 English synthesis; it is not a direct translation of the ancient source it discusses.

origin.excerpt: This account of P'an Ku and his achievements is of Taoist origin. The Buddhists have given a somewhat different account of him, which is a late adaptation from the Taoist myth, and must not be mistaken for Buddhist cosmogony proper.

narrativeBlocks.title: The giant inside the egg
narrativeBlocks.body: In the Taoist account, Chaos was a cosmic egg — and inside it grew P'an Ku, who spent eighteen thousand years chiseling it apart: the light, pure parts rose as Heaven, the heavy parts sank as Earth.

narrativeBlocks.title: Holding the sky apart
narrativeBlocks.body: Fearing the two would collapse back together, P'an Ku stands between them — pushing Heaven up and Earth down, growing taller every day for another eighteen thousand years until the separation holds.

narrativeBlocks.title: The body that became the world
narrativeBlocks.body: When at last he dies, his breath becomes wind and clouds, his voice thunder, his left eye the sun and right eye the moon, his limbs the mountains, his blood the rivers, his hair the stars and plants.

narrativeBlocks.title: A creation made of a body
narrativeBlocks.body: Unlike a word-spoken creation, this cosmos is literally built out of one giant's body — the world as the remains of a sacrifice.

narrativeBlocks.title: A written-down folk story
narrativeBlocks.body: The account survives through later Chinese scholarship — a literary synthesis of what may be much older folk material. We hold the details at arm's length but the shape is real.

quiz.prompt: How does P'an Ku make Heaven and Earth?

choices.text: He molds them from river clay
He calls them into being with a word
He chisels apart the cosmic egg for eighteen thousand years — the light parts rise, the heavy parts sink
He carves them from a mountain

quiz.explanation: The egg's two halves become sky and ground — the oldest Chinese creation account.

quiz.prompt: What does P'an Ku's body become at death?

choices.text: The world's features — breath to wind, eyes to sun and moon, limbs to mountains, blood to rivers
The gods of the four directions

quiz.explanation: The cosmos is literally built from him — the world as his remains.
